title_eng: Practical delta check limits for tumour markers in different clinical settings
abstract:
Objectives: Few studies have reported on delta checks for
tumour markers, even though these markers are often
evaluated serially. Therefore, this study aimed to establish a
practical delta check limit in di ﬀerent clinical settings
for ﬁve tumour markers: alpha-fetoprotein, cancer antigen
19-9, cancer antigen 125, carcinoembryonic antigen, and
prostate-speciﬁc antigen.
Methods: Pairs of patients ’ results (current and previous)
for ﬁve tumour markers between 2020 and 2021 were
retrospectively collected from three university hospitals. The
data were classi ﬁed into three subgroups, namely: health
check-up recipient (subgroup H), outpatient (subgroup O),
and inpatient (subgroup I) clinics. The check limits of delta
percent change (DPC), absolute DPC (absDPC), and reference
change value (RCV) for each test were determined using the
development set (the ﬁrst 18 months, n=179,929) and then
validated and simulated by applying the validation set (the
last 6 months, n=66,332).
Results: The check limits of DPC and absDPC for most tests
varied signi ﬁcantly among the subgroups. Likewise, the
proportions of samples requiring further evaluation, calcu-
lated by excluding samples with both current and previous
results within the reference intervals, were 0.2 – 2.9% (lower
limit of DPC), 0.2 – 2.7% (upper limit of DPC), 0.3 – 5.6%
(absDPC), and 0.8 – 35.3% (RCV 99.9%). Furthermore, high
negative predictive values >0.99 were observed in all
subgroups in the in silico simulation.
Conclusions: Using real-world data, we found that DPC was
the most appropriate delta-check method for tumour
markers. Moreover, Delta-check limits for tumour markers
should be applied based on clinical settings.

Introduction
Delta check, a rule used to as sess laboratory data for
potential errors, is a crucial pos t-analytical electronic tool
in laboratory quality managem ent systems [1]. Tradition-
ally, a delta check compares sequential laboratory results
and a predetermined limit [1]. Delta check values
exceeding the predetermined limit may not be due to
biological or analytical vari ations [1], but due to errors
more broadly within the test ing process such as misiden-
tiﬁcation, intravenous ﬂuid contamination, falsely low or
high results related to specimen quality, and data entry
error [2]. Frequently used delta check methods are based
on the distribution of delta values in the patient popula-
tion: delta di ﬀerence (DD), delta percent change (DPC),
rate di ﬀerence (RD), and rate percent change (RPC). DD
denotes the di ﬀerence between the most recent and
previous results. DPC denotes the proportion of the DD
divided by the previous results, and RD and RPC are

calculated by dividing the DD and DPC by the time interval
between the current and previous testing times, respec-
tively. Delta check limits can also be calculated via -
biological variations. For example, the reference change
value (RCV) can be calculated using within-subject bio-
logical variation (CV I) and analytical imprecision (CV A)
estimates [3].
Tumour markers, including alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), carci-
noembryonic antigen (CEA), cancer antigen 125 (CA 125), cancer
antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), and prostate-speciﬁca n t i g e n( P S A ) ,h a v e
been used in the diagnosis and monitoring of various cancers.
Increased AFP levels are associated with poor prognoses and
recurrence of hepatocellular carcinomas [4– 6]. CA 19-9 is a
biomarker for ovarian cancer, along with CA 125, and pancreatic
cancer [7, 8], while CEA is generally used to monitor gastroin-
testinal cancers [9]. Studies on delta check limits have mainly
focused on chemistry tests, withfew studies focusing on tumour
markers [10], which might be because more data are needed to
assess their eﬀectiveness. For the measurands with a low index
of individuality (<0.6) for a cor rect interpretation of serial
results, the use of the RIs should be replaced by the RCV, based
on CVI, whereas tests with a high index of individuality (>1.4)
are not [3, 11]. Therefore, these measurands might be suitable
to undergo delta check using limits RCV based. Based on a
previously reported index of individuality data such as AFP
(0.07– 0.1), CA 19-9 (0.07– 0.13), CA 125 (0.18– 0.21), CEA (0.11– 0.14),
and PSA (0.16– 0.25) [12– 15], we considered all tumour markers
suitable for investigating delta check.
Changes in laboratory results of patients are not
substantial during routine examinations or in ambulatory
care, while those of unwell and hospitalized patients are
considerable upon disease diagnosis or after therapy [2].
Therefore, separately obtaining the delta check limit based
on the clinical status of patients might be a reasonable
approach. However, because there are con ﬂicting
information concerning the e ﬃcacy and yield of delta
checks during quality control tests due to the low
automation error rates observed [16], laboratories must
review the utility of their current delta check practices, as
they may be ine ﬀective [17]. Moreover, excessive or ‘false
alarm’ delta checks increase unnecessary retesting, sta ﬀ
ineﬃciency, and turnaround time (TAT) [18]. Therefore, an
acceptable delta limit must be set for each laboratory to
avoid delays in reporting results by ideally using laboratory
data from their respective patient population. However,
setting up and reviewing laboratory-speci ﬁc delta check
limits is not always possible.
Therefore, this study aimed to establish practical,
laboratory-appropriate delta limits for use in health check-ups,
outpatient, and inpatient clinical settings, for ﬁve frequently
assessed tumour markers: AFP, CA 19-9, CA 125, CEA, and PSA.
Materials and methods
Study design and data collection
This study was conducted at three university-a ﬃliated hospitals in the
Republic of Korea: the Pusan National University Hospital, with 1,290 beds;
the Haeundae Paik Hospital in Busan, with 969 beds; and the Ilsan Paik
Hospital in Goyang, with 731 beds. Five tumour markers were investigated

This study was approved by our Institutional Review board
(2210-023-120, HPIRB 2022-09-017, ISPAIK 2022-09-031) and was
performed in accordance with the tenets of the Helsinki ’s Declaration
and its amendments (as revised in 2013). The requirement for informed
consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study. A ﬂow
diagram of the study process is shown in Figure 1.
All tumour markers were measured using Roche Cobas C-8000 (Roche
diagnostics, GmbH, Mannheim, Germany) instrument with a dedicated
calibrator and reagents (Elecsys AFP, Elecsys CA 19-9, Elecsys CA 125 II,
Elecsys CEA, and Elecsys total PSA; Roche diagnostics, GmbH, Mannheim,
Germany). The analytical measurement ranges were as follows:
0.908– 1,210 μg/L for AFP, 0.6– 1,000 KU/L for CA 19-9, 0.6– 5,000 KU/L for CA
125, 0.2– 1,000 μg/L for CEA, and 0.003 – 100 μg/L for PSA. The reference
intervals (RIs) were≤7.0 μg/L for AFP, ≤34 KU/L for CA 19-9, ≤35 KU/L for
CA 125, and ≤4.3 μg/L for CEA. The RIs for PSA were ≤1.4 μg/L for patients
aged <40 years,≤2.0 μg/L for patients aged between 40 and 49 years,≤3.1 μg/
L for patients aged between 50 and 59 years, ≤4.1 μg/L for patients
aged between 60 and 69 years, and≤4.4 μg/L for patients aged≥70 years.
Selection of delta check methods
We calculated the coeﬃcient of variation (CV) (%) of the absolute delta

absDD and the time interval for each tumour marker within each subgroup
(Supplementary Table 1). To select the best delta check method among DD,
DPC, RD, and RPC, we used the same cut-oﬀ values for the CV% of the absDD
